topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: How is a pure equipment failure of a navigation system normally shown?

options.text: By the autopilot disconnecting with no indication
By a gradual drift of the position only
By a call from ATC
By a warning light

explanation: Modern INS and radio navigation installations of two or three sets include comparators and warnings; a pure equipment failure is shown by a warning light.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: In a three-set navigation system, how is an inaccurate unit found?

options.text: It cannot be found until landing
By switching all three off and on
By comparing the three outputs (voting)
By asking ATC for a radar position

explanation: With three systems the outputs are compared, a voting system in which an error in any one set is quickly detected.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: Why is a fault harder to find in a two-set navigation system?

options.text: A disagreement does not show which is wrong
Two-set systems have no warning lights
Two-set systems cannot be compared at all
Two-set systems only work over land

explanation: With two sets, a disagreement shows that one is wrong but not which one, unless the system displays malfunction codes. An independent fix is needed to decide.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: How can a crew decide which of two disagreeing navigation systems is wrong?

options.text: By averaging the two positions
By checking both against an independent fix
By using the system that was switched on first
By choosing the system on the commander's side

explanation: A fix from weather radar, ADF/NDB bearings or a VOR, compared with the system positions, should reveal the inaccurate one.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: If no fix is available, which basic cross-check can help identify a faulty navigation system?

options.text: Asking the cabin crew to look outside
Comparing the fuel used with the plan
Comparing winds, ground speed and drift with nearby aircraft
Comparing the clock times on both systems

explanation: Basic methods include contacting another aircraft nearby to compare spot winds, ground speed and drift; as a last resort, compare with the forecast wind at the DR position.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
subtopic: Unable to comply with the clearance
question: An aircraft can no longer continue as cleared. What should it do whenever possible?

options.text: Descend to FL100 at once
Continue and explain after landing
Turn back immediately without telling ATC
Get a revised clearance before acting

explanation: Whenever possible, a revised clearance must be obtained before initiating any action, including when the aircraft cannot keep the required navigation accuracy.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
subtopic: Unable to comply with the clearance
question: How should a revised clearance be requested when an aircraft cannot continue as cleared?

options.text: Through the operator's company frequency
By distress or urgency procedures
Only by datalink message
By squawking 7600 and waiting

explanation: The revised clearance is obtained using radiotelephony distress or urgency traffic as appropriate; ATC then acts on the pilot's intentions and the traffic situation.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: Above what latitude are polar tracks generally considered to be?
explanation: Polar tracks involve navigation at high latitudes, above about 65°N.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: Why are magnetic compasses unreliable near the magnetic pole?

options.text: The aircraft's radios interfere at high latitude
Steep dip and rapidly changing variation
There are no magnetic fields at the pole
The cold stops the compass liquid moving

explanation: Steep magnetic dip and high rates of change of variation make magnetic compasses unreliable and magnetic north impractical as a reference.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: How is navigation usually achieved in polar regions?

options.text: By grid navigation, inertial systems and GPS
By dead reckoning from the forecast wind only
By magnetic compass and VOR radials
By NDB bearings only

explanation: Navigation is achieved by grid navigation and reliance on inertial and satellite systems.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: To what are VORs in the far north of Canada aligned?

options.text: Grid north
Magnetic north
The local runway direction
True north

explanation: Near the north magnetic pole, where variation changes rapidly, VORs (for example in the Canadian Northern Control Area) are oriented to true north to assist grid navigation.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: Why must crews regularly check autopilot engagement on long-range flights?

options.text: The autopilot always fails after 3 hours
The autopilot cannot fly at night
It can drop out of steering mode unnoticed
The autopilot uses too much fuel

explanation: The autopilot can become unobtrusively disconnected from the steering mode in several ways, so regular checks of correct engagement are needed.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: When are present position coordinates recommended to be plotted after passing a waypoint?

options.text: About 10 minutes after each waypoint
At each waypoint exactly, as the aircraft passes overhead
Only when ATC asks
Every hour

explanation: It is recommended to display coordinates throughout and plot them about 10 minutes after each waypoint, to check the aircraft is on its cleared track.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: Why must crews be especially alert when low bank angles (around 10°) are used?

options.text: The autopilot will disconnect
Fuel use increases sharply
The aircraft may stall
Slow drifts off track may be missed

explanation: With low bank angles for passenger comfort, insidious departures from the cleared track are more likely, so close monitoring is essential.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: Which of these makes polar navigation difficult?

options.text: Too many ground navigation aids
Communications mainly limited to HF
Dense traffic at low level
Strong VHF signals interfering with the HF radios

explanation: Other difficulties include communications mainly on HF, few en route alternates and high rates of gyro correction for earth rate and transport wander.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: Which gyro corrections are particularly large at high latitude?

options.text: Deviation and variation
Pitch and roll error
Earth rate and transport wander
Turn error and acceleration error

explanation: High rates of gyro correction for earth rate and transport wander are a feature of polar flight.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: Which navigation technique is used with a directional gyro to solve polar navigation problems?

options.text: Radio range flying
Grid navigation
Magnetic heading flying
Pilotage

explanation: Grid navigation with a directional gyro, using polar stereographic charts, is used to overcome polar navigation problems.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: What is a minimum time route?

options.text: The quickest route within ATC limits
The great circle route in all cases
The route with the fewest waypoints
The shortest distance between two points

explanation: A minimum time route is the track that gives the shortest time between two points while respecting ATC and airspace restrictions.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: What is the shortest distance between two points on the earth?

options.text: A line of constant true track
The rhumb line
The minor arc of the great circle
The major arc of the great circle

explanation: Geographically, the shortest distance is the minor arc of the great circle joining the points; winds and restrictions may make another route quicker.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: Why may the minimum time route be longer than the great circle?

options.text: Great circles are always over water
Aircraft cannot fly great circles
Longer routes always use less fuel
Winds and restrictions can favour a longer track

explanation: Restricted areas, airways and especially winds can make a longer track the quickest option.

topic: 08 Long Range Flight and Polar Navigation
question: How are minimum time routes worked out today?

options.text: By hand, using three or four trial tracks each hour
By ATC for each aircraft
By computer
By the commander during the flight

explanation: Historically, they were worked out by hand from several trial tracks over successive hours; today all minimum time routes are computer-generated, which is quicker and more accurate.
